entries.bafc156385053513a3bcffec96b6fc8fa4db2c71: <div sID="gen20587" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Hab.2" sID="Hab.2"/> <div eID="gen20587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20588" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20589" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have an answer expected by the prophet (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">ver. 1</reference>), and returned by the Spirit of God, to the complaints which the prophet made of the violences and victories of the Chaldeans in the close of the foregoing chapter. The answer is, I. That after God has served his own purposes by the prevailing power of the Chaldeans, has tried the faith and patience of his people, and distinguished between the hypocrites and the sincere among them, he will reckon with the Chaldeans, will humble and bring down, not only that proud monarch Nebuchadnezzar, but that proud monarchy, for their boundless and insatiable thirst after dominion and wealth, for which they themselves should at length be made a prey, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.2-Hab.2.8">ver. 2-8</reference>. II. That not they only, but all other sinners like them, should perish under a divine woe. 1. Those that are covetous, are greedy of wealth and honours, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.9">ver. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.11">11</reference>. 2. Those that are injurious and oppressive, and raise estates by wrong and rapine, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.12-Hab.2.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. 3. Those that promote drunkenness that they may expose their neighbours to shame, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.15-Hab.2.17">ver. 15-17</reference>. 4. Those that worship idols, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.18-Hab.2.20">ver. 18-20</reference>.
entries.7ef148819239dd6503083a737ac42299b48645ec: <div eID="gen20589" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20588" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Waiting upon God; The People Directed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 600.)</title> <div sID="gen20590" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer when I am reproved. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make <hi type="italic">it</hi> plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it. <hi type="super">3</hi> For the vision <hi type="italic">is</hi> yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry. <hi type="super">4</hi> Behold, his soul <hi type="italic">which</hi> is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith. <div eID="gen20590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20591" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The prophet humbly gives his attendance upon God (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will stand upon my watch,</hi> as a sentinel on the walls of a besieged city, or on the borders of an invaded country, that is very solicitous to gain intelligence. I will look up, will look round, will look within, <hi type="italic">and watch to see what he will say unto me,</hi> will listen attentively to the words of his mouth and carefully observe the steps of his providence, that I may not lose the least hint of instruction or direction. <hi type="italic">I will watch to see what he will say in me</hi>" (so it may be read), "what the Spirit of prophecy in me will dictate to me, by way of answer to my complaints." Even in a ordinary way, God not only speaks to us by his word, but speaks in us by our own consciences, whispering to us, <hi type="italic">This is the way, walk in it;</hi> and we must attend to the voice of God in both. The prophet's standing upon his <hi type="italic">tower,</hi> or high place, intimates his prudence, in making use of the helps and means he had within his reach to know the mind of God, and to be instructed concerning it. Those that expect to hear from God must withdraw from the world, and get above it, must raise their attention, fix their thought, study the scriptures, consult experiences and the experienced, continue instant in prayer, and thus set themselves <hi type="italic">upon the tower.</hi> His standing upon his watch intimates his patience, his constancy and resolution; he will wait the time, and weather the point, as a watchman does, but he will have an answer; he will know what God will <hi type="italic">say to him,</hi> not only for his own satisfaction, but to enable him as a prophet to give satisfaction to others, and answer their exceptions, when he is reproved or argued with. Herein the prophet is an example to us. 1. When we are tossed and perplexed with doubts concerning the methods of Providence, are tempted to think that it is fate, or fortune, and not a wise God, that governs the world, or that the church is abandoned, and God's covenant with his people cancelled and laid aside, then we must take pains to furnish ourselves with considerations proper to clear this matter; we must stand upon our watch against the temptation, that it may not get ground upon us, must set ourselves upon the tower, to see if we can discover that which will silence the temptation and solve the objected difficulties, must do as the psalmist, <hi type="italic">consider the days of old</hi> and make <hi type="italic">a diligent search</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.6">Ps. lxxvii. 6</reference>), must go into the sanctuary of God, and there labour to understand the end of these things (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.17">Ps. lxxiii. 17</reference>); we must not give way to our doubts, but struggle to make the best of our way out of them. 2. When we have been at prayer, pouring out our complaints and requests before God, we must carefully observe what answers God gives by his word, his Spirit, and his providences, to our humble representations; when David says, <hi type="italic">I will direct my prayer unto thee,</hi> as an arrow to the mark, he adds, <hi type="italic">I will look up,</hi> will look after my prayer, as a man does after the arrow he has shot, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.3">Ps. v. 3</reference>. We must <hi type="italic">hear what God the Lord will speak,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.85.8">Ps. lxxxv. 8</reference>. 3. When we go to read and hear the word of God, and so to consult the lively oracles, we must set ourselves to observe what God will thereby <hi type="italic">say unto us,</hi> to suit our case, what word of conviction, caution, counsel, and comfort, he will bring to our souls, that we may receive it, and submit to the power of it, and may consider what we shall answer, what returns we shall make to the word of God, when we are reproved by it. 4. When we are attacked by such as quarrel with God and his providence as the prophet here seems to have been—beset, besieged, as in a tower, by hosts of objectors—we should consider how to answer them, fetch our instructions from God, hear what he says to us for our satisfaction, and have that ready to say to others, <hi type="italic">when we are reproved,</hi> to satisfy them, as a <hi type="italic">reason of the hope that is in us</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.15">1 Pet. iii. 15</reference>), and beg of God <hi type="italic">a mouth and wisdom,</hi> and that it may be <hi type="italic">given us in that same hour what we shall speak.</hi> <div eID="gen20591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20592" type="x-p"/> II. God graciously gives him the meeting; for he will not disappoint the believing expectations of his people that wait to hear what he will say unto them, but will <hi type="italic">speak peace,</hi> will <hi type="italic">answer them with good words and comfortable words,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.1.13">Zech. i. 13</reference>. The prophet had complained of the prevalence of the Chaldeans, which God had given him a prospect of; now, to pacify him concerning it, he here gives him a further prospect of their fall and ruin, as Isaiah, before this, when he had foretold the captivity in Babylon, foretold also the destruction of Babylon. Now, this great and important event being made known to him by a vision, care is taken to publish the vision, and transmit it to the generations to come, who should see the accomplishment of it. <div eID="gen20592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20593" type="x-p"/> 1. The prophet must <hi type="italic">write the vision,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.2">v. 2</reference>. Thus, when St. John had a vision of the New Jerusalem, he was ordered to <hi type="italic">write,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.21.5">Rev. xxi. 5</reference>. He must write it, that he might imprint it on his own mind, and make it more clear to himself, but especially that it might be notified to those in distant places and transmitted to those in future ages. What is handed down by tradition is easily mistaken and liable to corruption; but what is written is reduced to a certainty, and preserved safe and pure. We have reason to bless God for written visions, that God has written to us the great things of his prophets as well as of his law. He must <hi type="italic">write the vision,</hi> and <hi type="italic">make it plain upon tables,</hi> must write it legibly, in large characters, so that <hi type="italic">he who runs may read it,</hi> that those who will not allow themselves leisure to read it deliberately may not avoid a <hi type="italic">cursory</hi> view of it. Probably, the prophets were wont to write some of the most remarkable of their predictions in tables, and to hang them up in the temple, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.1">Isa. viii. 1</reference>. Now the prophet is told to <hi type="italic">write this</hi> very <hi type="italic">plain.</hi> Note, Those who are employed in preaching the word of God should study plainness as much as may be, so as to make themselves intelligible to the meanest capacities. The things of our everlasting peace, which God has written to us, are made plain, <hi type="italic">they are all plain to him that understands</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.9">Prov. viii. 9</reference>), and they are published with authority; God himself has prefixed his <hi type="italic">imprimatur</hi> to them; he has said, <hi type="italic">Make them plain.</hi> <div eID="gen20593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20594" type="x-p"/> 2. The people must wait for the accomplishment of the <hi type="italic">vision</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The vision is yet for an appointed time</hi> to come. You shall now be told of your deliverance by the breaking of the Chaldeans' power, and that the time of it is fixed in the counsel and decree of God. <hi type="italic">There is an appointed time,</hi> but it is not near; it is yet to be deferred a great while;" and that comes in here as a reason why it must be written, that it may be reviewed afterwards and the event compared with it. Note, God has an appointed time for his appointed work, and will be sure to do the work when the time comes; it is not for us to anticipate his appointments, but to wait his time. And it is a great encouragement to wait with patience, that, though the promised favour be deferred long, it will come at last, and be an abundant recompence to us for our waiting: <hi type="italic">At the end it shall speak and not lie.</hi> We shall not be disappointed of it, for it will come at the time appointed; nor shall we be disappointed in it, for it will fully answer our believing expectations. The promise may seem silent a great while, but at the end it shall speak; and therefore, <hi type="italic">though it tarry</hi> longer than we expected, yet we must continue <hi type="italic">waiting for it,</hi> being assured it will come, and willing to tarry until it does come. The day that God has set for the deliverance of his people, and the destruction of his and their enemies, is a day, (1.) That will surely come at last; it is never adjourned <hi type="italic">sine die—without fixing another day,</hi> but it will without fail come at the fixed time and the fittest time. (2.) It <hi type="italic">will not tarry,</hi> for God <hi type="italic">is not slack, as some count slackness</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.9">2 Pet. iii. 9</reference>); <hi type="italic">though it tarry</hi> past our time, yet <hi type="italic">it does not tarry</hi> past God's time, which is always the best time. <div eID="gen20594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20595" type="x-p"/> 3. This vision, the accomplishment of which is so long waited for, will be such an exercise of faith and patience as will try and discover men what they are, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.4">v. 4</reference>. (1.) There are some who will proudly disdain this vision, whose hearts are so lifted up that they scorn to take notice of it; if God will work for them immediately, they will thank him, but they will not give him credit; their hearts are lifted up towards vanity, and, since God puts them off, they will shift for themselves and not be beholden to him; they think <hi type="italic">their own hands sufficient for them,</hi> and God's promise is to them an insignificant thing. That man's soul that is thus <hi type="italic">lifted up is not upright in him;</hi> it is not right with God, is not as it should be. Those that either distrust or despise God's all-sufficiency will not walk uprightly with him, <reference osisRef="Gen.17.1">Gen. xvii. 1</reference>. But, (2.) Those who are truly good, and whose hearts are upright with God, will value the promise, and venture their all upon it; and, in confidence of the truth of it, will keep close to God and duty in the most difficult trying times, and will then live comfortably in communion with God, dependence on him, and expectation of him. <hi type="italic">The just shall live by faith;</hi> during the captivity good people shall support themselves, and live comfortably, by faith in these precious promises, while the performance of them is deferred. <hi type="italic">The just shall live by his faith,</hi> by that faith which he acts upon the word of God. This is quoted in the New Testament (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.17">Rom. i. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.11">Gal. iii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">Heb. x. 38</reference>), for the proof of the great doctrine of justification by faith only and of the influence which the grace of faith has upon the Christian life. Those that are made <hi type="italic">just by faith shall live,</hi> shall be happy here and for ever; while they are here, they live by it; when they come to heaven faith shall be swallowed up in vision.
entries.a197ab89abef365a50ec8c928eb668edc1a68467: <div eID="gen20595" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgment Predicted; Judgment of the King of Babylon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 600.)</title> <div sID="gen20596" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Yea also, because he transgresseth by wine, <hi type="italic">he is</hi> a proud man, neither keepeth at home, who enlargeth his desire as hell, and <hi type="italic">is</hi> as death, and cannot be satisfied, but gathereth unto him all nations, and heapeth unto him all people: <hi type="super">6</hi> Shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb against him, and say, Woe to him that increaseth <hi type="italic">that which is</hi> not his! how long? and to him that ladeth himself with thick clay! <hi type="super">7</hi> Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee, and awake that shall vex thee, and thou shalt be for booties unto them? <hi type="super">8</hi> Because thou hast spoiled many nations, all the remnant of the people shall spoil thee; because of men's blood, and <hi type="italic">for</hi> the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein. <hi type="super">9</hi> Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the power of evil! <hi type="super">10</hi> Thou hast consulted shame to thy house by cutting off many people, and hast sinned <hi type="italic">against</hi> thy soul. <hi type="super">11</hi> For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it. <hi type="super">12</hi> Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and stablisheth a city by iniquity! <hi type="super">13</hi> Behold, <hi type="italic">is it</hi> not of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts that the people shall labour in the very fire, and the people shall weary themselves for very vanity? <hi type="super">14</hi> For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , as the waters cover the sea. <div eID="gen20596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20597" type="x-p"/> The prophet having had orders to <hi type="italic">write the vision,</hi> and the people to wait for the accomplishment of it, the vision itself follows; and it is, as divers other prophecies we have met with, the burden of Babylon and Babylon's king, the same that was said to <hi type="italic">pass over</hi> and <hi type="italic">offend,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.1.11">ch. i. 11</reference>. It reads the doom, some think, of Nebuchadnezzar, who was principally active in the destruction of Jerusalem, or of that monarchy, or of the whole kingdom of the Chaldeans, or of all such proud and oppressive powers as bear hard upon any people, especially upon God's people. Observe, <div eID="gen20597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20598" type="x-p"/> I. The charge laid down against this enemy, upon which the sentence is grounded, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">v. 5</reference>. The <hi type="italic">lusts of the flesh, the lusts of the eye,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the pride of life,</hi> are the entangling snares of men, and great men especially; and we find him that led Israel captive himself led captive by each of these. For, 1. He is sensual and voluptuous, and given to his pleasures: <hi type="italic">He transgresses by wine.</hi> Drunkenness is itself a transgression, and is the cause of abundance of transgression. We read of those that <hi type="italic">err through wine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.28.7">Isa. xxviii. 7</reference>. Belshazzar (in whom particularly this prophecy had its accomplishment) was in the height of his transgression by wine when the hand-writing upon the wall signed the warrant for his immediate execution, pursuant to this sentence, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.1">Dan. v. 1</reference>. 2. He is haughty and imperious: <hi type="italic">He is a proud man,</hi> and his pride is a certain presage of his fall coming on. If great men be proud men, the great God will make them know he is above them. His transgressing by wine is made the cause of his arrogance and insolence: therefore <hi type="italic">he is a proud man.</hi> When a man is drunk, though he makes himself as mean as a beast, yet he thinks himself as great as a king, and prides himself in that by which he shames himself. We find <hi type="italic">the crown of pride</hi> upon the head of the <hi type="italic">drunkards of Ephraim,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">woe</hi> to both, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">Isa. xxviii. 1</reference>. 3. He is covetous and greedy of wealth, and this is the effect of his pride; he thinks himself worthy to enjoy all, and therefore makes it his business to engross all. The Chaldean monarchy aimed to be a universal one. He <hi type="italic">keeps not at home,</hi> is not content with his own, which he has an incontestable title to, but thinks it too little, and so enjoys it not, nor takes the comfort he might in his own palace, in his own dominion. His sin is his punishment, his ambition is his perpetual uneasiness. Though the home be a palace, yet to a discontented mind it is a prison. He <hi type="italic">enlarges his desire as hell,</hi> or <hi type="italic">the grave,</hi> which daily receives the body of the dead, and yet still cries, <hi type="italic">Give, give;</hi> he is <hi type="italic">as death,</hi> which continues to devour, and <hi type="italic">cannot be satisfied.</hi> Note, It is the sin and folly of many who have a great deal of the wealth of this world that they do not know when they have enough, but the more they have the more they would have, and the more eager they are for it. And it is just with God that the desires which are insatiable should still be unsatisfied; it is the doom passed on those that <hi type="italic">love silver</hi> that they shall never be <hi type="italic">satisfied with it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.10">Eccl. v. 10</reference>. Those that will not be content with their allotments shall not have the comfort of their achievements. This proud prince is still <hi type="italic">gathering to him all nations, and heaping to him all people,</hi> invading their rights, seizing their properties, and they must not be unless they will be his, and under his command. One nation will not satisfy him unless he has another, and then another, and all at last; as those in a lower sphere, to gratify the same inordinate desire, lay <hi type="italic">house to house, and field to field, that they may be placed alone in the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.5.8">Isa. v. 8</reference>. And it is hard to say which is more to be pitied, the folly of such ambitious princes as place their honour in enlarging their dominions, and not in ruling them well, or the misery of those nations that are harassed and pulled to pieces by them. <div eID="gen20598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20599" type="x-p"/> II. The sentence passed upon him (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Shall not all these take up a parable against him?</hi> His doom is, <div eID="gen20599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20600" type="x-p"/> 1. That, since pride has been his sin, disgrace and dishonour shall be his punishment, and he shall be loaded with contempt, shall be laughed at and despised by all about him, as those that look big, and aim high, deserve to be, and commonly are, when they are brought down and baffled. <div eID="gen20600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20601" type="x-p"/> 2. That, since he has been abusive to his neighbours, those very persons whom he has abused shall be the instruments of his disgrace: <hi type="italic">All those shall take up a taunting proverb against him.</hi> They shall have the pleasure of insulting over him and he the shame of being trampled upon by them. Those that shall triumph in the fall of this great tyrant are here furnished with a <hi type="italic">parable,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">taunting proverb,</hi> to take up against him. <hi type="italic">He shall say</hi> (he that draws up the insulting ditty shall say thus), <hi type="italic">Ho, he that increases that which is not his! Aha!</hi> what has become of him now? So it may be read in a taunting way. Or, <hi type="italic">He shall say,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">the just,</hi> who <hi type="italic">lives by his faith,</hi> he to whom the vision is written and made plain, with the help of that shall say this, shall foretel the enemy's fall, even when he sees him flourishing, and <hi type="italic">suddenly curse his habitation,</hi> even when he is <hi type="italic">taking root,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.5.3">Job v. 3</reference>. He shall indeed denounce woes against him. <div eID="gen20601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20602" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is a woe against him for increasing his own possessions by invading his neighbour's rights, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.6-Hab.2.8">v. 6-8</reference>. He <hi type="italic">increases that which is not his,</hi> but other people's. Note, No more of what we have is to be reckoned ours than what we came honestly by; nor will it long be ours, for <hi type="italic">wealth gotten by vanity will be diminished.</hi> Let not those that thrive in the world be too forward to bless themselves in it, for, if they do not thrive lawfully, they are under a woe. See here, [1.] What this prosperous prince is doing; he is <hi type="italic">lading himself with thick clay.</hi> Riches are but clay, thick clay; what are gold and silver but white and yellow earth? Those that travel through thick clay are both retarded and dirtied in their journey; so are those that go through the world in the midst of an abundance of the wealth of it; but, as if that were not enough, what fools are those that <hi type="italic">load themselves with it,</hi> as if this trash would be their treasure! They burden themselves with continual care about it, with a great deal of guilt in getting, saving, and spending it, and with a heavy account which they must give of it another day. They overload their ship with this thick clay, and so sink it and themselves <hi type="italic">into destruction and perdition.</hi> [2.] See what people say of him, while he is thus increasing his wealth; they cry, "<hi type="italic">How long?</hi> How long will it be ere he has enough?" They cry to God, "How long wilt thou suffer this proud oppressor to trouble the nations?" Or they say to one another, "See how long it will last, how long he will be able to keep what he gets thus dishonestly." They dare not speak out, but we know what they mean when they say, <hi type="italic">How long?</hi> [3.] See what will be in the end hereof. What he has got by violence from others, others shall take by violence from him. The Medes and Persians shall make a prey of the Chaldeans, as they have done of other nations, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.7-Hab.2.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. "There shall be those that will <hi type="italic">bite thee</hi> and <hi type="italic">vex thee;</hi> those from whom thou didst not fear any danger, that seemed <hi type="italic">asleep,</hi> shall <hi type="italic">rise up</hi> and <hi type="italic">awake</hi> to be a plague to thee. They shall rise up <hi type="italic">suddenly</hi> when thou are most secure, and least prepared to receive the shock and ward off the blow. <hi type="italic">Shall they not rise up suddenly?</hi> No doubt they shall, and thou thyself hast reason to expect it, to be dealt with as thou hast dealt with others, that <hi type="italic">thou shalt be for booties unto them,</hi> as others have been unto thee, that, according to the law of retaliation, as <hi type="italic">thou hast spoiled many nations</hi> so thou shalt thyself be <hi type="italic">spoiled</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.8">v. 8</reference>); <hi type="italic">all the remnant of the people shall spoil thee.</hi>" The king of Babylon thought he had brought all the nations round about him so low that none of them would be able to make reprisals upon him; but though they were but a remnant of people, a very few left, yet these shall be sufficient to spoil him, when God has such a controversy with him, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> For <hi type="italic">men's blood,</hi> and the thousands of lives that have been sacrificed to his ambition and revenge, especially for the blood of Israelites, which is in a special manner precious to God. <hi type="italic">Secondly, For the violence of the land,</hi> his laying waste so many countries, and destroying the fruits of the earth, especially in the land of Israel. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> For the violence <hi type="italic">of the city,</hi> the many cities that he had turned into ruinous heaps, especially Jerusalem the holy city, and of <hi type="italic">all that dwelt therein,</hi> who were ruined by him. Note, The violence done by proud men to advance and enrich themselves will be called over again (and must be accounted for) another day, by him <hi type="italic">to whom vengeance belongs.</hi> <div eID="gen20602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20603" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is a woe against him for coveting still more, and aiming to be still higher, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.9-Hab.2.11">v. 9-11</reference>. The crime for which this woe is denounced is much the same with that in the foregoing article—an insatiable desire of wealth and honour; it is <hi type="italic">coveting an evil covetousness to his house,</hi> that is, grasping at an abundance for his family. Note, Covetousness is a very evil thing in a family; it brings disquiet and uneasiness into it (<hi type="italic">he that is greedy of gain troubles his own house</hi>), and, which is worse, it brings the curse of God upon it and upon all the affairs of it. <hi type="italic">Woe to him that gains an evil gain;</hi> so the margin reads it. There is a lawful gain, which by the blessing of God may be a comfort to a house (<hi type="italic">a good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children</hi>), but what is got by fraud and injustice is ill-got, and will be poor gain, will not only do no good to a family, but will bring poverty and ruin upon it. Now observe, [1.] What this covetous wretch aims at; it is <hi type="italic">to set his nest on high,</hi> to raise his family to some greater dignity than it had before arrived at, or to set it, as he apprehends, out of the reach of danger, that he may be <hi type="italic">delivered from the power of evil,</hi> that it may not be in the power of the worst of his enemies to do him a mischief nor so much as to disturb his repose. Note, It is common for men to pretend it as an excuse for their covetousness and ambition that they only consult their own safety, and aim to secure themselves; and yet they do but deceive themselves when they think <hi type="italic">their wealth</hi> will be a <hi type="italic">strong city</hi> to them, <hi type="italic">and a high wall,</hi> for it is so only <hi type="italic">in their own conceit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.11">Prov. xviii. 11</reference>. [2.] What he will get by it: <hi type="italic">Thou hast consulted,</hi> not safety, but <hi type="italic">shame, to thy house, by cutting off many people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.10">v. 10</reference>. Note, An estate raised by iniquity is a scandal to a family. Those that cut off, or undermine, others, to make room for themselves, that impoverish others to enrich themselves, do but consult shame to their houses, and fasten upon them a mark of infamy. Yet that is not the worst of it: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast sinned against thy own soul,</hi> hast brought that under guilt and wrath, and endangered that." Note, Those that do wrong to their neighbour do a much greater wrong to their own souls. But if the sinner pleads, Not guilty, and thinks he has managed his frauds and violence with so much art and contrivance that they cannot be proved upon him, let him know that if there be no other witnesses against him <hi type="italic">the stone shall cry out of the wall</hi> against him, and <hi type="italic">the beam out of the timber</hi> in the roof <hi type="italic">shall answer it,</hi> shall second it, shall witness it, that the money and materials wherewith he built the house were unjustly gotten, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.11">v. 11</reference>. The stones and timber cry to heaven for vengeance, as <hi type="italic">the whole creation groans under</hi> the sin of man and waits to be delivered from that <hi type="italic">bondage of corruption.</hi> <div eID="gen20603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20604" type="x-p"/> (3.) Here is a woe against him for building a town and a city by blood and extortion (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.12">v. 12</reference>): He <hi type="italic">builds a town,</hi> and is him-self lord of it; he <hi type="italic">establishes a city,</hi> and makes it his royal seat. So Nebuchadnezzar did (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.30">Dan. iv. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">Is not this great Babylon that I have built for the house of the kingdom?</hi> But it is built with the blood of his own subjects, whom he has oppressed, and the blood of his neighbours, whom he has unjustly invaded; it is <hi type="italic">established by iniquity,</hi> by the unrighteous laws that are made for the security of it. <hi type="italic">Woe</hi> to him that does so; for the towns and cities thus built can never be established; they will fall, and their founders be buried in the ruins of them. Babylon, which was built by blood and iniquity, did not continue long; its day soon came to fall; and then this woe took effect, when that prophecy, which is expressed as a history (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.9">Isa. xxi. 9</reference>), proved a history indeed: <hi type="italic">Babylon has fallen, has fallen!</hi> And the destruction of that city was, [1.] The shame of the Chaldeans, who had taken so much pains, and were at such a vast expense, to fortify it (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Is it not of the Lord of hosts that the people</hi> who have laboured so hard to defend that city shall <hi type="italic">labour in the very fire,</hi> shall see the out-works which they confided in the strength of set on fire, and shall labour in vain to save them? Or they, in their pursuits of worldly wealth and honour, put themselves to great fatigue, and ran a great hazard, as those that <hi type="italic">labour in the fire</hi> do. The worst that can be said of the labourers in God's vineyards is that <hi type="italic">they have borne the burden and heat of the day</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.12">Matt. xx. 12</reference>); but those that are eager in their worldly pursuits <hi type="italic">labour in the very fire,</hi> make themselves perfect slaves to their lusts. There is not a greater drudge in the world than he that is under the power of reigning covetousness. And what comes of it? Though they take a world of pains they are but poorly paid for it; for, after all, <hi type="italic">they weary themselves for very vanity;</hi> they were told it was vanity, and when they find themselves disappointed of it, and disappointed in it, they will own it is worse than vanity, it is <hi type="italic">vexation of spirit.</hi> [2.] It was the honour of God, as a God of impartial justice and irresistible power; for by the ruin of the Chaldean monarchy (which all the world could not but take notice of) <hi type="italic">the earth was filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.14">v. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord is known by</hi> these <hi type="italic">judgments which he executes,</hi> especially when he is pleased to <hi type="italic">look upon proud men and abase them,</hi> for he thereby proves himself to be <hi type="italic">God alone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.40.11-Job.40.12">Job xl. 11, 12</reference>. See what good God brings out of the staining and sinking of earthly glory; he thereby manifests and magnifies his own glory, and <hi type="italic">fills the earth</hi> with the knowledge of it as plentifully as the <hi type="italic">waters cover the sea,</hi> which lie deep, spread far, and shall not be dried up until time shall be no more. Such is the <hi type="italic">knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ</hi> given by the gospel (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2 Cor. iv. 6</reference>), and such was the knowledge of his glory by the miraculous ruin of Babylon. Note, Such as will not be taught the knowledge of God's glory by the judgments of his mouth shall be made to know and acknowledge it by the judgments of his hand.
entries.7d416d64179897f7b0636637110287594e7bc66b: <div eID="gen20604" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgment Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 600.)</title> <div sID="gen20605" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, that puttest thy bottle to <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and makest <hi type="italic">him</hi> drunken also, that thou mayest look on their nakedness! <hi type="super">16</hi> Thou art filled with shame for glory: drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered: the cup of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's right hand shall be turned unto thee, and shameful spewing <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> on thy glory. <hi type="super">17</hi> For the violence of Lebanon shall cover thee, and the spoil of beasts, <hi type="italic">which</hi> made them afraid, because of men's blood, and for the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein. <hi type="super">18</hi> What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols? <hi type="super">19</hi> Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise, it shall teach! Behold, it <hi type="italic">is</hi> laid over with gold and silver, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no breath at all in the midst of it. <hi type="super">20</hi> But the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him. <div eID="gen20605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20606" type="x-p"/> The three foregoing articles, upon which the woes here are grounded, are very near akin to each other. The criminals charged by them are oppressors and extortioners, that raise estates by rapine and injustice; and it is mentioned here again (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.17">v. 17</reference>), the very same that was said <reference osisRef="Hab.2.8">v. 8</reference>, for that is the crime upon which the greatest stress is laid; it is <hi type="italic">because of men's blood,</hi> innocent blood, barbarously and unjustly shed, which is a provoking crying thing; it is <hi type="italic">for the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein,</hi> which God will certainly reckon for, sooner or later, as the asserter of right and the avenger of wrong. <div eID="gen20606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20607" type="x-p"/> But here are two articles more, of a different nature, which carry a <hi type="italic">woe</hi> to all those in general to whom they belong, and particularly to the Babylonian monarchs, by whom the people of God were taken and held captives. <div eID="gen20607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20608" type="x-p"/> I. The promoters of drunkenness stand here impeached and condemned. Belshazzar was one of those; he was so, remarkably that very night that the prophecy of this chapter was fulfilled in the period of his life and kingdom, when he <hi type="italic">drank wine before a thousand</hi> of his lords (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.1">Dan. v. 1</reference>), began the healths, and forced them to pledge him. And perhaps it was one reason why the succeeding monarchs of Persia made it a law of their kingdom that <hi type="italic">in drinking none should compel,</hi> but <hi type="italic">they should do according to every man's pleasure</hi> (as we find, <reference osisRef="Esth.1.8">Esth. i. 8</reference>), because they had seen in the kings of Babylon the mischievous consequences of forcing healths and making people drunk. But the woe here stands firm and very fearful against all those, whoever they are, who are guilty of this sin at any time, and in any place, from the stately palace (where that was) to the paltry ale-house. Observe, <div eID="gen20608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20609" type="x-p"/> 1. Who the sinner is that is here articled against; it is he that <hi type="italic">makes his neighbour drunk,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.15">v. 15</reference>. To give a neighbour drink who is in want, who is thirsty and poor, though it be but a cup of cold water to a disciple, in the name of a disciple, to give drink to weary traveller, nay, and to give strong drink to him that is ready to perish, and wine to those that are heavy of heart, is a piece of charity which is required of us, and shall be recompensed to us. <hi type="italic">I was thirsty, and you gave me drink.</hi> But to give a neighbour drink who has enough already, and more than enough, with design to intoxicate him, that he may expose himself, may talk foolishly, and make himself ridiculous, may disclose his own secret concerns, or be drawn in to agree to a bad bargain for himself—this is abominable wickedness; and those who are guilty of it, who make a practice of it, and take a pride and pleasure in it, are rebels against God in heaven, and his sacred laws, factors for the devil in hell, and his cursed interests, and enemies to men on earth, and their honour and welfare; they are like the son of Nebat, who <hi type="italic">sinned and made Israel to sin.</hi> To entice others to drunkenness, to <hi type="italic">put the bottle to them,</hi> that they may be allured to it by its charms, by <hi type="italic">looking on the wine when it is red and gives its colour in the cup,</hi> or to force them to it, obliging them by the rules of the club (and club-laws indeed they are) to drink so many glasses, and so filled, is to do what we can, and perhaps more than we know of, towards the murder both of soul and body; and those that do so have a great deal to answer for. <div eID="gen20609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20610" type="x-p"/> 2. What the sentence is that is here passed upon him. There is a woe to him (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.15">v. 15</reference>), and a punishment (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.16">v. 16</reference>) that shall answer to the sin. (1.) Does he put the cup of drunkenness into the hand of his neighbour? The cup of fury, the cup of trembling, the <hi type="italic">cup of the Lord's right hand,</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">turned unto him;</hi> the power of God shall be armed against him. That cup which had gone round among the nations, to make them <hi type="italic">a desolation, an astonishment, and a hissing,</hi> which had made them stumble and <hi type="italic">fall,</hi> so that they could <hi type="italic">rise no more,</hi> shall at length be put into the hand of the king of Babylon, as was foretold, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.15-Jer.25.16 Jer.25.18 Jer.25.26 Jer.25.27">Jer. xxv. 15, 16, 18, 26, 27</reference>. Thus the New-Testament Babylon, which had made the nations drunk with the cup of her fornications, shall <hi type="italic">have blood given her to drink, for she is worthy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.18.3">Rev. xviii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.6">6</reference>. (2.) Does he take a pleasure in putting his neighbour to shame? He shall himself be loaded with contempt: "<hi type="italic">Thou art filled with shame for glory, with shame instead of glory,</hi> or art filled now with shame more than ever thou wast with glory; and the glory thou hast been filled with shall but serve to make thy shame the more grievous to thyself, and the more ignominious in the eyes of others. Thou <hi type="italic">also shalt drink</hi> of the cup of trembling, and shalt expose thyself by thy fear and cowardice, which shall be as the <hi type="italic">uncovering of thy nakedness,</hi> to thy shame; and all about thee shall load thee with disgrace, for <hi type="italic">shameful spewing shall be on thy glory,</hi> on that which thou hast most prided thyself in, thy dignity, wealth, and dominion; those whom thou hast made drunk shall themselves spew upon it. For <hi type="italic">the violence of Lebanon shall cover thee, and the spoil of beasts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.17">v. 17</reference>); thou shalt be hunted and run down with as much violence as ever any wild beasts in Lebanon were, shall be spoiled as they are, and thy fall made a sport of; for thou art as one of the beasts that made them afraid, and therefore they triumph when they have got the mastery of thee." Or, "It is because of the violence thou hast done to Lebanon, that is, the land of Israel (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.25">Deut. iii. 25</reference>) and the temple (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.1">Zech. xi. 1</reference>), that God now reckons with thee; that is the sin that now covers thee." <div eID="gen20610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20611" type="x-p"/> II. The promoters of idolatry stand here impeached and condemned; and this also was a sin that Babylon was notoriously guilty of; it was the <hi type="italic">mother of harlots.</hi> Belshazzar, in his revels, <hi type="italic">praised his idols.</hi> And for this, here is a woe against them, and in them against all others that do likewise, particularly the New-Testament Babylon. Now see here, <div eID="gen20611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20612" type="x-p"/> 1. What they do to promote idolatry; they are <hi type="italic">mad upon their idols;</hi> so the Chaldeans are said to be, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.38">Jer. l. 38</reference>. For, (1.) They have a great variety of idols, their <hi type="italic">graven images</hi> and <hi type="italic">molten images,</hi> that people may take their choice, which they like best. (2.) They are very nice and curious in the framing of them: The <hi type="italic">maker of the work</hi> has performed his part admirably well, the <hi type="italic">fashioner of his fashion</hi> (so it is in the margin), that contrived the model in the most significant manner. (3.) They are at great expense in beautifying and adorning them: <hi type="italic">They lay them over with gold and silver;</hi> because these are things people love and dote upon wherever they meet with them, they dress up their idols in them, the more effectually to court the adoration of the children of this world. (4.) They have great expectations from them: <hi type="italic">The maker of the work trusts therein</hi> as his god, puts a confidence in it, and gives honour to it as his god. The worshippers of God give honour to him, by offering up their prayers to him, and waiting to receive instructions and directions from him; and these honours they give to their idols. [1.] They pray to them: <hi type="italic">They say to the wood, Awake</hi> for our relief, "awake to hear our prayers;" and to the dumb stone, "<hi type="italic">Arise,</hi> and save us," as the church prays to her God, <hi type="italic">Awake, O Lord! arise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.44.23">Ps. xliv. 23</reference>. They own their image to be a god by praying to it. <hi type="italic">Deliver me, for thou art my God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.17">Isa. xliv. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">Deos qui rogat ille facit—That to which a man addresses petitions is to him a god.</hi> [2.] They consult them as oracles, and expect to be directed and dictated to by them: <hi type="italic">They say to the dumb stone,</hi> though it cannot speak, <hi type="italic">yet it shall teach.</hi> What the wicked demon, or no less wicked priest, speaks to them from the image, they receive with the utmost veneration, as of divine authority, and are ready to be governed by it. Thus is idolatry planted and propagated under the specious show of religion and devotion. <div eID="gen20612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20613" type="x-p"/> 2. How the extreme folly of this is exposed. God, by Isaiah, when he foretold the deliverance of his people out of Babylon, largely showed the shameful stupidity and sottishness of idolaters, and so he does here by the prophet, on the like occasion. (1.) Their images, when they have made them, are but mere matter, which is the meanest lowest rank of being; and all the expense they are at upon them cannot advance them one step above that. They are wholly void both of sense and reason, lifeless and speechless (the idol is a <hi type="italic">dumb idol,</hi> a <hi type="italic">dumb stone,</hi> and there is <hi type="italic">no breath at all in the midst of it</hi>), so that the most minute animal, that has but breath and motion, is more excellent then they. They have not so much as the spirit of a beast. (2.) It is not in their power to do their worshippers any good (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">What profits the graven image?</hi> Though it be mere matter, if it were cast into some other form it might be serviceable to some purpose or other of human life; but, as it is made a god of, it is of no profit at all, nor can do its worshippers the least kindness. Nay, (3.) It is so far from profiting them that it puts a cheat upon them, and keeps them under the power of a strong delusion; they say, <hi type="italic">It shall teach,</hi> but it is a <hi type="italic">teacher of lies;</hi> for it represents God as having a body, as being finite, visible, and dependent, whereas he is a Spirit, infinite, invisible, and independent, and it confirms those that become vain in their imaginations in the false notions they have of God, and makes the idea of God to be a precarious thing, and what every man pleases. If we may say to the <hi type="italic">works of our hands, You are our gods,</hi> we may say so to any of the creatures of our own fancy, though the chimera be ever so extravagant. An image is a <hi type="italic">doctrine of vanities;</hi> it is <hi type="italic">falsehood,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">work of errors,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.10.8">Jer. x. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.14">14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.15">15</reference>. It is therefore easy to see what the religion of those is, and what they aim at, who recommend those teachers of lies as laymen's books, which they are to study and govern themselves by, when they have locked up from them the book of the scriptures in an unknown tongue. <div eID="gen20613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20614" type="x-p"/> 3. How the people of God triumph in him, and therewith support themselves, when the idolaters thus shame themselves (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">But the Lord is in his holy temple.</hi> (1.) <hi type="italic">Our rock is not as their rock,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.31">Deut. xxxii. 31</reference>. Theirs are dumb idols; ours is Jehovah, a living God, who is what he is, and not, as theirs, what men please to make him. He is in his holy temple in heaven, the residence of his glory, where we have access to him in the way, not which we have invented, but which he himself has instituted. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.115.3">Ps. cxv. 3</reference>, <hi type="italic">But our God is in the heavens,</hi> and <reference osisRef="Ps.11.4">Ps. xi. 4</reference>. (2.) The multitude of their gods which they set up, and take so much pains to support, cannot thrust out our God; he is, and will be, in his holy temple still, and glorious in holiness. They have laid waste his temple at Jerusalem; but he has a temple above that is out of the reach of their rage and malice, but within the reach of his people's faith and prayers. (3.) Our God will make all the world silent before him, will strike the idolaters as dumb as their idols, convincing them of their folly, and covering them with shame. He will silence the fury of the oppressors, and check their rage against his people. (4.) It is the duty of his people to attend him with silent adorings (<reference osisRef="Ps.65.1">Ps. lxv. 1</reference>), and patiently to wait for his appearing to save them in his own way and time. <hi type="italic">Be still, and know that he is God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.2.13">Zech. ii. 13</reference>.  <chapter eID="Hab.2"/> <div eID="gen20614" type="x-p"/>

entries.8a628e124c2a3f6a0719d84cfa98e62108e45b88: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12883"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hab.2.1-Hab.2.20">Ha 2:1-20</reference>. The Prophet, Waiting Earnestly for an Answer to His Complaints (First Chapter), Receives a Revelation, Which Is to Be Fulfilled, Not Immediately, Yet in Due Time, and Is Therefore to Be Waited for in Faith: The Chaldeans Shall Be Punished for Their Cruel Rapacity, nor Can Their False GodS Avert the Judgment of Jehovah, the Only True God.</title> <div sID="gen24039" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12883"/><hi type="bold">1. stand upon ... watch--</hi>that is, watch-post. The prophets often compare themselves, awaiting the revelations of Jehovah with earnest patience, to watchmen on an eminence watching with intent eye all that comes within their view (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.8">Is 21:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.21.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.17">Jr 6:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.17">Eze 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.2">33:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.3">3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.5.3">Psa 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.85.8">85:8</reference>). The "watch-post" is the withdrawal of the whole soul from earthly, and fixing it on heavenly, things. The accumulation of synonyms, "stand upon ... watch ... set me upon ... tower ... watch to see" implies persevering fixity of attention.<div eID="gen24039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24040" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what he will say unto me--</hi>in answer to my complaints (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.13">Ha 1:13</reference>). Literally, "in me," God speaking, not to the prophet's outward ear, but inwardly. When we have prayed to God, we must observe what answers God gives by His word, His Spirit, and His providences.<div eID="gen24040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24041" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what I shall answer when I am reproved--</hi>what answer I am to make to the reproof which I anticipate from God on account of the liberty of my expostulation with Him. Maurer translates, "What I am to answer in respect to my complaint against Jehovah" (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.12-Hab.1.17">Ha 1:12-17</reference>). <div eID="gen24041" type="x-p"/>
entries.40a30091a57cbf485bef6d19bdb6ba9c7e40468a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12884"/><div sID="gen24042" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12884"/><hi type="bold">2. Write the vision--</hi>which I am about to reveal to thee.<div eID="gen24042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make it plain--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.27.8">De 27:8</reference>). In large legible characters.<div eID="gen24043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon tables--</hi>boxwood tables covered with wax, on which national affairs were engraved with an iron pen, and then hung up in public, at the prophets' own houses, or at the temple, that those who passed might read them. Compare <reference osisRef="Luke.1.63">Lu 1:63</reference>, "writing table," that is, tablet.<div eID="gen24044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that he may run that readeth it--</hi>commonly explained, "so intelligible as to be easily read by any one running past"; but then it would be, "that he that runneth may read it." The true sense is, "so legible that whoever readeth it, may run to tell all whom he can the good news of the foe's coming doom, and Judah's deliverance." Compare <reference osisRef="Dan.12.4">Da 12:4</reference>, "many shall run to and fro," namely, with the explanation of the prophecy, then unsealed; also, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.17">Re 22:17</reference>, "let him that heareth (the good news) say (to every one within his reach), Come." "Run" is equivalent to announce the divine revelation (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.21">Jr 23:21</reference>); as everyone who becomes informed of a divine message is bound to run, that is, use all despatch to make it known to others [Henderson]. Grotius, Ludovicus De Dieu, and Maurer interpret it: "Run" is not literal running, but "that he who reads it may run through it," that is, read it at once without difficulty. <div eID="gen24045" type="x-p"/>
entries.96dc9a4313064465e3f74e6c76299d67e9a62625: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12885"/><div sID="gen24046" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12885"/><hi type="bold">3. for--</hi>assigning the cause why it ought to be committed to writing: because its fulfilment belongs to the future.<div eID="gen24046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24047" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the vision is yet for an appointed time--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.10.14">Da 10:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.27">11:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.35">35</reference>). Though the time appointed by God for the fulfilment be yet future, it should be enough for your faith that God hath spoken it (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.26">La 3:26</reference>).<div eID="gen24047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24048" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at the end it shall speak--</hi>Maurer translates, "it pants for the end." But the antithesis between, "it shall speak," and "not be silent," makes English Version the better rendering. So the Hebrew is translated in <reference osisRef="Prov.12.17">Pr 12:17</reference>. Literally, "breathe out words," "break forth as a blast."<div eID="gen24048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24049" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">though it tarry, wait for it--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.49.18">Ge 49:18</reference>). <div eID="gen24049" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4116e30fd8ab8478919b0cee9ce97d2c0e4bc49: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12886"/><div sID="gen24050" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12886"/><hi type="bold">4. his soul which is lifted up--</hi>the Chaldean's [Maurer]. The unbelieving Jew's [Henderson].<div eID="gen24050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is not upright in him--</hi>that is, is not accounted upright in God's sight; in antithesis to "shall live." So <reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">He 10:38</reference>, which with inspired authority applies the general sense to the particular case which Paul had in view, "If any man draw back (one result of being 'lifted up' with overweening arrogancy), my soul shall have no pleasure in him."<div eID="gen24051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24052" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the just shall live by his faith--</hi>the Jewish nation, as opposed to the unbelieving Chaldean (compare <reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Ha 2:5</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Hab.1.6">Ha 1:6</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Hab.1.13">Ha 1:13</reference>) [Maurer]. Henderson's view is that the believing Jew is meant, as opposed to the unbelieving Jew (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.1.17">Ro 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.11">Ga 3:11</reference>). The believing Jew, though God's promise tarry, will wait for it; the unbelieving "draws back," as <reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">He 10:38</reference> expresses it. The sense, in Maurer's view, which accords better with the context (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Ha 2:5</reference>, &c.). is: the Chaldean, though for a time seeming to prosper, yet being lifted up with haughty unbelief (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.11">Ha 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>), is not upright; that is, has no right stability of soul resting on God, to ensure permanence of prosperity; hence, though for a time executing God's judgments, he at last becomes "lifted up" so as to attribute to his own power what is the work of God, and in this sense "draws back" (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.38">He 10:38</reference>), becoming thereby a type of all backsliders who thereby incur God's displeasure; as the believing Jew is of all who wait for God's promises with patient faith, and so "live" (stand accepted) before God. The Hebrew accents induce Bengel to translate, "he who is just by his faith shall live." Other manuscripts read the accents as English Version, which agrees better with Hebrew syntax. <div eID="gen24052" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1964c672b11453e3ef58cf3b6a97cf6a0fc277f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12887"/><div sID="gen24053" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12887"/><hi type="bold">5. Yea also, because--</hi>additional reason why the Jews may look for God punishing their Chaldean foe, namely, because ... he is<div eID="gen24053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a proud man--</hi>rather, this clause continues the reason for the Jews expecting the punishment of the Chaldeans, "because he transgresseth by wine (a besetting sin of Babylon, compare <reference osisRef="Dan.5.1-Dan.5.31">Da 5:1-31</reference>, and Curtius [5.1]), being a proud man." Love of wine often begets a proud contempt of divine things, as in Belshazzar's case, which was the immediate cause of the fall of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.2-Dan.4.30">Da 5:2-4, 30</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Prov.20.1">Pr 20:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.9">30:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.31.5">31:5</reference>).<div eID="gen24054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24055" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enlargeth his desire as hell--</hi>the grave, or the unseen world, which is "never full" (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.20">Pr 27:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.16">30:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.14">Is 5:14</reference>). The Chaldeans under Nebuchadnezzar were filled with an insatiable desire of conquest. Another reason for their punishment. <div eID="gen24055" type="x-p"/>
entries.06e3aae65607d7130a14aef4b66050fbae7fdeee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12888"/><div sID="gen24056" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12888"/><hi type="bold">6. Shall not all these--</hi>the "nations" and "peoples" (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Ha 2:5</reference>) "heaped unto him" by the Chaldean.<div eID="gen24056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24057" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take up a parable--</hi>a derisive song. Habakkuk follows Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.4">Is 14:4</reference>) and Micah (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.4">Mi 2:4</reference>) in the phraseology.<div eID="gen24057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against him--</hi>when dislodged from his former eminence.<div eID="gen24058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Woe--</hi>The "derisive song" here begins, and continues to the end of the chapter. It is a symmetrical whole, and consists of five stanzas, the first three consisting of three verses each, the fourth of four verses, and the last of two. Each stanza has its own subject, and all except the last begin with "Woe"; and all have a closing verse introduced with "for," "because," or "but."<div eID="gen24059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24060" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how long?--</hi>how long destined to retain his ill-gotten gains? But for a short time, as his fall now proves [Maurer]. "Covetousness is the greatest bane to men. For they who invade others' goods, often lose even their own" [Menander]. Calvin makes "how long?" to be the cry of those groaning under the Chaldean oppression while it still lasted: How long shall such oppression be permitted to continue? But it is plainly part of the derisive song, after the Chaldean tyranny had passed away.<div eID="gen24060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ladeth himself with thick clay--</hi>namely, gold and silver dug out of the "clay," of which they are a part. The covetous man in heaping them together is only lading himself with a clay burden, as he dares not enjoy them, and is always anxious about them. Lee and Fuller translate the Hebrew as a reduplicated single noun, and not two words, "an accumulation of pledges" (<reference osisRef="Deut.24.10-Deut.24.13">De 24:10-13</reference>). The Chaldean is compared to a harsh usurer, and his ill-gotten treasures to heaps of pledges in the hands of a usurer. <div eID="gen24061" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc92a4e3ea73473f69021bb63327afd45c3d8445: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12889"/><div sID="gen24062" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12889"/><hi type="bold">7. suddenly--</hi>the answer to the question, "How long?" (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.6">Ha 2:6</reference>).<div eID="gen24062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24063" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bite--</hi>often used of usury; so favoring Lee's rendering (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.6">Ha 2:6</reference>). As the Chaldean, like a usurer, oppressed others, so other nations shall, like usurers, take pledges of, that is, spoil, him. <div eID="gen24063" type="x-p"/>
entries.011819fc6ffba36d68ebd493d6e907cc290c07f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12890"/><div sID="gen24064" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12890"/><hi type="bold">8. the remnant of the people--</hi>Those remaining of the peoples spoiled by thee, though but a remnant, will suffice to inflict vengeance on thee.<div eID="gen24064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the violence of the land ... city--</hi>that is, on account of thy violent oppression of the lands and cities of the earth [Grotius] (compare <reference osisRef="Hab.2.5">Ha 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.12">6, 12</reference>). The same phrase occurs in <reference osisRef="Hab.2.17">Ha 2:17</reference>, where the "land" and "city" are Judea and Jerusalem. <div eID="gen24065" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff4e95d0f2f377994bedda3e75c8319f2d2962ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12891"/><div sID="gen24066" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12891"/><hi type="bold">9. coveteth an evil covetousness--</hi>that is, a covetousness so surpassingly evil as to be fatal to himself.<div eID="gen24066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to his house--</hi>greedily seizing enormous wealth, not merely for himself, but for his family, to which it is destined to be fatal. The very same "evil covetousness" that was the cause of Jehoiakim's being given up to the Chaldean oppressor (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.13">Jr 22:13</reference>) shall be the cause of the Chaldean's own destruction.<div eID="gen24067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24068" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set his nest on high--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Num.24.21">Nu 24:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.16">Jr 49:16</reference>; Ob 4). The image is from an eagle (<reference osisRef="Job.39.27">Job 39:27</reference>). The royal citadel is meant. The Chaldean built high towers, like the Babel founders, to "be delivered from the power of evil" (<reference osisRef="Gen.11.4">Ge 11:4</reference>). <div eID="gen24068" type="x-p"/>
entries.94ad2e64d206f7760d6666425902a9cb1f8cd42f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12892"/><div sID="gen24069" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12892"/><hi type="bold">10. Thou hast consulted shame ... by cutting off many--</hi>Maurer, more literally, "Thou hast consulted shame ... to destroy many," that is, in consulting (determining) to cut off many, thou hast consulted shame to thy house.<div eID="gen24069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24070" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sinned against thy soul--</hi>that is, against thyself; thou art the guilty cause of thine own ruin (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.36">Pr 8:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.2">20:2</reference>). They who wrong their neighbors, do much greater wrong to their own souls. <div eID="gen24070" type="x-p"/>
entries.64c70d37a03085d161ca1e7acbfaf28ae9e84726: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12893"/><div sID="gen24071" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12893"/><hi type="bold">11. stone ... cry out--</hi>personification. The very stones of thy palace built by rapine shall testify against thee (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.40">Lu 19:40</reference>).<div eID="gen24071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the beam out of the timber--</hi>the crossbeam or main rafter connecting the timbers in the walls.<div eID="gen24072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall answer it--</hi>namely, the stone. The stone shall begin and the crossbeam continue the cry against thy rapine. <div eID="gen24073" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e52ae5a22d1ce4c07e1c2b3826cb8c59404c8f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12894"/><div sID="gen24074" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12894"/><hi type="bold">12. buildeth a town with blood--</hi>namely, Babylon rebuilt and enlarged by blood-bought spoils (compare <reference osisRef="Dan.4.30">Da 4:30</reference>). <div eID="gen24074" type="x-p"/>
entries.c9cdb6a4916abea18cfbddce72ce85b223d0396a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12895"/><div sID="gen24075" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12895"/><hi type="bold">13. is it not of the Lord of hosts--</hi>Jehovah, who has at His command all the hosts of heaven and earth, is the righteous author of Babylon's destruction. "Shall not God have His turn, when cruel rapacious men have triumphed so long, though He seem now to be still?" [Calvin].<div eID="gen24075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">people ... labour in the ... fire ... weary themselves for ... vanity--</hi>The Chaldeans labor at what is to be food for the fire, namely, their city and fortresses which shall be burnt. <reference osisRef="Jer.51.58">Jr 51:58</reference> adopts the same phraseology to express the vanity of the Chaldean's labor on Babylon, as doomed to the flames. <div eID="gen24076" type="x-p"/>
entries.df14704559931c469882ffcb3c08171034b703ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12896"/><div sID="gen24077" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12896"/>14. Adapted from <reference osisRef="Isa.11.9">Is 11:9</reference>. Here the sense is, "The Jews shall be restored and the temple rebuilt, so that God's glory in saving His people, and punishing their Chaldean foe, shall be manifested throughout the world," of which the Babylonian empire formed the greatest part; a type of the ultimate full manifestation of His glory in the final salvation of Israel and His Church, and the destruction of all their foes.<div eID="gen24077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24078" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">waters cover the sea--</hi>namely, the bottom of the sea; the sea-bed. <div eID="gen24078" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f3685785b09d014cc25ddd0b303e5a2dfc7f661: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12897"/><div sID="gen24079" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12897"/><hi type="bold">15. giveth ... neighbour drink ... puttest ... bottle to him--</hi>literally, "skin," as the Easterns use "bottles" of skin for wine. Maurer, from a different Hebrew root, translates, "that pourest in thy wrath." English Version keeps up the metaphor better. It is not enough for thee to be "drunken" thyself, unless thou canst lead others into the same state. The thing meant is, that the Chaldean king, with his insatiable desires (a kind of intoxication), allured neighboring states into the same mad thirst for war to obtain booty, and then at last exposed them to loss and shame (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.51.17">Is 51:17</reference>; Ob 16). An appropriate image of Babylon, which at last fell during a drunken revel (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.1-Dan.5.31">Da 5:1-31</reference>).<div eID="gen24079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24080" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that thou mayest look on their nakedness!--</hi>with light, like Ham of old (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.22">Ge 9:22</reference>). <div eID="gen24080" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ef45e975e01bca557da3330e16b63175b2bd2de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12898"/><div sID="gen24081" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12898"/><hi type="bold">16. art filled--</hi>now that thou art fallen. "Thou art filled" indeed (though so insatiable), but it is "with shame."<div eID="gen24081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24082" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shame for glory--</hi>instead of thy former glory (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.7">Ho 4:7</reference>).<div eID="gen24082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24083" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drink thou also--</hi>The cup of sorrow is now in thy turn to pass to thee (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.15-Jer.25.17">Jr 25:15-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.21">La 4:21</reference>).<div eID="gen24083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24084" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy foreskin--</hi>expressing in Hebrew feeling the most utter contempt. So of Goliath (<reference osisRef="1Sam.17.36">1Sa 17:36</reference>). It is not merely thy "nakedness," as in <reference osisRef="Hab.2.15">Ha 2:15</reference>, that shall be "uncovered," but the foreskin, the badge of thy being an uncircumcised alien from God. The same shall be done to thee, as thou didst to others, and worse.<div eID="gen24084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24085" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cup ... shall be turned unto thee--</hi>literally, "shall turn itself," namely, from the nations whom thou hast made to drink it. "Thou shalt drink it all, so that it may be turned as being drained" [Grotius].<div eID="gen24085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24086" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shameful spewing--</hi>that is, vomiting; namely, that of the king of Babylon, compelled to disgorge the spoil he had swallowed. It expresses also the ignominious state of Babylon in its calamity (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.27">Jr 25:27</reference>). "Be drunken, spew, and fall." Less appropriately it is explained of the foe spewing in the face of the Babylonian king. <div eID="gen24086" type="x-p"/>
entries.3cef39dca2d6d3979321afc3edaa9bc65787a561: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12899"/><div sID="gen24087" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12899"/><hi type="bold">17. the violence of Lebanon--</hi>thy "violence" against "Lebanon," that is, Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.24">Is 37:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.23">Jr 22:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.12">12</reference>; for Lebanon's cedars were used in building the temple and houses of Jerusalem; and its beauty made it a fit type of the metropolis), shall fall on thine own head.<div eID="gen24087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24088" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cover--</hi>that is, completely overwhelm.<div eID="gen24088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24089" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the spoil of beasts, which made them afraid--</hi>Maurer explains, "the spoiling inflicted on the beasts of Lebanon (that is, on the people of Jerusalem, of which city 'Lebanon' is the type), which made them afraid (shall cover thee)." But it seems inappropriate to compare the elect people to "beasts." I therefore prefer explaining, "the spoiling of beasts," that is, such as is inflicted on beasts caught in a net, and "which makes them afraid (shall cover thee)." Thus the Babylonians are compared to wild beasts terrified at being caught suddenly in a net. In cruel rapacity they resembled wild beasts. The ancients read, "the spoiling of wild beasts shall make THEE afraid." Or else explain, "the spoiling of beasts (the Medes and Persians) which (inflicted by thee) made them afraid (shall in turn cover thyself--revert on thyself from them)." This accords better with the parallel clause, "the violence of Lebanon," that is, inflicted by thee on Lebanon. As thou didst hunt men as wild beasts, so shalt thou be hunted thyself as a wild beast, which thou resemblest in cruelty.<div eID="gen24089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because of men's blood--</hi>shed by thee; repeated from <reference osisRef="Hab.2.8">Ha 2:8</reference>. But here the "land" and "city" are used of Judea and Jerusalem: not of the earth and cities generally, as in <reference osisRef="Hab.2.8">Ha 2:8</reference>.<div eID="gen24090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the violence of the land, &c.--</hi>that is, inflicted on the land by thee. <div eID="gen24091" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf1a195e02a9e6c9ada53cbe571ef556a66c49b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12900"/><div sID="gen24092" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12900"/>18. The powerlessness of the idols to save Babylon from its doom is a fitting introduction to the last stanza (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.19">Ha 2:19</reference>), which, as the former four, begins with "Woe."<div eID="gen24092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">teacher of lies--</hi>its priests and prophets uttering lying oracles, as if from it.<div eID="gen24093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make dumb idols--</hi>Though men can "make" idols, they cannot make them speak. <div eID="gen24094" type="x-p"/>
entries.debe9da3e13d2078f8da7c70642597375f3348a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12901"/><div sID="gen24095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12901"/><hi type="bold">19. Awake--</hi>Arise to my help.<div eID="gen24095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24096" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it shall teach!--</hi>rather, An exclamation of the prophet, implying an ironical question to which a negative answer must be given. What! "It teach?" Certainly not [Maurer]. Or, "It (the idol itself) shall (that is, ought to) teach you that it is deaf, and therefore no God" [Calvin]. Compare "they are their own witnesses" (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.9">Is 44:9</reference>).<div eID="gen24096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24097" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Behold--</hi>The Hebrew is nominative, "There it is" [Henderson].<div eID="gen24097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24098" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it is laid over with gold ... no breath ... in the midst--</hi>Outside it has some splendor, within none. <div eID="gen24098" type="x-p"/>
entries.ceb7bd9e39d33d42e434f7de3e682bbf9ecd5352: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12902"/><div sID="gen24099" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12902"/><hi type="bold">20. But the Lord--</hi>Jehovah; in striking contrast with the idols.<div eID="gen24099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in his holy temple--</hi>"His place" (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">Is 26:21</reference>); heaven (<reference osisRef="Ps.11.4">Psa 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.7">Jon 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.1.2">Mi 1:2</reference>). The temple at Jerusalem is a type of it, and there God is to be worshipped. He does not lie hid under gold and silver, as the idols of Babylon, but reigns in heaven and fills heaven, and thence succors His people.<div eID="gen24100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24101" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">keep silence--</hi>in token of reverent submission and subjection to His judgments (<reference osisRef="Job.40.4">Job 40:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.76.8">Psa 76:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.7">Zep 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.2.13">Zec 2:13</reference>). <chapter eID="Hab.2"/>
